## Test Settings

!!! info "Time Estimate"
    - 2 hours to read the [Set Up](../setup/overview.md){: target="_blank" }, [Operate](../operation/loop/open-loop.md){: target="_blank" } and [FAQs](../faqs/overview-faqs.md){: target="_blank" } tabs and [LoopTips](https://loopkit.github.io/looptips/)
    - 1-3 days to test your settings
        * You can test after you build the *Loop* app, as long as you stay in [`Open Loop`](../operation/loop/open-loop.md)

!!! abstract "Summary"
    - Before you use <code>Closed Loop</code>, test your basal rates, insulin sensitivity factor (ISF) and carb ratio (CR)
    - You may need to change them for the *Loop* app
    - Accurate settings are vital for success

!!! question "FAQs"
    - **"My endo chose my settings. Do I still need to test them?"** Yes. Settings that work for traditional pump therapy may not be best for the *Loop* app. Even a couple of days of testing makes a big difference.
    - **"I have great control. Why test?"** Great control often comes from many small corrections, and those can hide settings that need to change. If you memorize your meal doses, you may not know your real CR or ISF.
    - **"I can't basal test my 2-year-old. What can I do?"** Talk with your endo, watch for patterns and do your best. Once you know the *Loop* app, you can fine-tune settings while staying in closed loop, as long as they are close.

The *Loop* app is a calculator: its answers are only as good as the settings you give it.

## Basal Rates

The right basal rates keep your glucose steady when you have not eaten. To test, wait at least 2 hours after eating, then watch your glucose for 4-6 relaxed hours without food. Does it stay steady, climb or drop? Basal rates also decide how much of your insulin counts as insulin on board (IOB).

!!! tip "Basal Tricks"
    The *Loop* app tracks how much more or less insulin than your scheduled basal rates you need. Once you know the app, you can tune your basal rates by watching IOB overnight or at other times without food or exercise.

## Insulin Sensitivity Factor

The Insulin Sensitivity Factor (ISF), also called correction factor, is how much one unit of insulin lowers your glucose. A higher number means you are more sensitive to insulin. An ISF of 50 mg/dL (2.8 mmol/L) means one unit lowers your glucose by 50 mg/dL (2.8 mmol/L) when basal rates are correct and there is no food or activity.

Test ISF after you test your basal rates. Start when your glucose is above target, for example after a glucose tab or when you are stuck high.

* Take the insulin needed to bring you to target, and check whether your glucose levels off at target within 3 hours
    * Do not test after eating, after treating a low, after exercise, or when you are sick or stressed
* If you have no idea where to start, divide 1800 by your total daily dose
    * Example: 30 U a day gives a starting ISF of 60 mg/dL (3.3 mmol/L)
    * Many people end up higher or lower than this starting point

## Carb Ratio

The Carb Ratio (CR) is the grams of carbs covered by one unit of insulin. A good CR brings your glucose back near where it started within 3 hours *of the meal*. High-fat or high-protein meals can raise glucose for longer.

If you spike after meals but return to your starting glucose, try bolusing 15-20 minutes earlier before you change your CR.
